 Kailey Hagen, CFP®, The Motley Fool Sun, October 25, 2026 at 3:20 PM MST 4 min read If you're wondering how your Social Security check stacks up to the average, you're looking for a single benchmark. As of September 2026, the average monthly benefit for retired workers is $2,088.79, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA) Monthly Statistical Snapshot. That amounts to about $25,065.48 per year. 
 This figure is a broad average that spans every retired worker in the system, from 62-year-olds to those aged 99 and older. Because it covers such a wide range of people, your own check could look very different. The payment you receive depends heavily on your work history and when you claim.

 What the average really looks like 
 Age changes the math significantly. The average benefit for people aged 62 is just $1,424.40 per month, as of December 2025, the most recent data available. Meanwhile, the average for those aged 70 is $2,274.68. This gap exists because workers who wait to claim earn higher monthly payments for life. 
 Gender also plays a role in where you land relative to the benchmark. As of December 2025, according to the SSA, the average benefit for men is higher than the average for women. The table below shows the overall average for each group across all ages.

 How to beat the benchmark 
 To land above the average, the SSA looks at three main factors: how long you worked, how much you earned, and when you claimed. The SSA calculates your benefit based on your average wages across your 35 highest-earning years. It adjusts those earlier wages for inflation and runs them through the primary insurance amount (PIA) formula. 
 Full retirement age (FRA) ranges from 66 to 67, depending on your birth year, and it's 67 for everyone born in 1960 or later. If you claim at age 62, your PIA is reduced by up to 30%. Waiting until age 70 earns you delayed retirement credits, worth an 8% increase for every year you delay past your full retirement age. 
 Higher lifetime earnings and more years in the workforce also push your check upward. This isn't always within your control, as health issues or caregiving often interrupt a career. However, more years of work generally result in a higher calculation because the SSA doesn't have to fill your 35-year record with zeros. 
 Story Continues Even if you beat the average, Social Security probably won't cover everything. The system is designed to replace only about 40% of your pre-retirement income. Most retirees need significantly more than that to stay comfortable. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), the average household led by someone 65 or older spent $61,432 annually in 2024, the most recent year for which data is available. 
 Inflation adjustments help, but they don't solve the shortfall. A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) will take effect in 2027. The 3.6% COLA will add about $75 a month on top of the September 2026 average. Even with these raises, most retirees still rely on savings or other income sources to make ends meet. 
 Ultimately, beating the Social Security average is just a reference point; the real goal is covering your actual retirement expenses. 
 How Social Security fits into your retirement plan 
 Above-average Social Security checks are great, but knowing where you fall in relation to the average doesn't tell you what percentage of your retirement expenses your checks will cover. For that, you have to look at your own estimates of your retirement spending. 
 Some people spend less in retirement than they do throughout their careers, but this isn't universal. If you're someone who enjoys traveling, for example, you might spend more than you're used to during retirement. 
 You can estimate your future Social Security benefit at every claiming age by creating a my Social Security account and using the benefit estimator tool there. Once you have a rough idea of how much you'll get, subtract this from your estimated monthly retirement expenses. 
 Then, come up with a plan to cover the rest. This could include personal savings, a pension if you qualify for one, and maybe even a part-time job.
